title: Rich Dad Poor Dad Cashflow Quadrant and Tax Strategy
summary: Robert Kiyosaki and his CPA, Tom Wheelwright, explain the Cashflow Quadrant and how building assets using debt allows investors to achieve infinite ROI and minimize taxes. They claim that traditional education fails to teach practical financial literacy, leading people into high-tax employee and self-employed categories.
key_points: Taxes are the single largest expense for entrepreneurs and taxpayers.
The Cashflow Quadrant consists of four types of people in business: Employee (E), Self-Employed (S), Business Owner (B), and Investor (I).
Employees (E) pay about 40 percent tax, Self-Employed (S) pay about 60 percent tax, Business Owners (B) with 500+ employees pay about 20 percent tax, and Investors (I) pay 0 percent tax.
Assets put money in your pocket, while liabilities take money out of your pocket.
The creator claims debt is good when used to buy assets because it generates cash flow and tax benefits, such as depreciation and amortization.
ROI stands for Return on Information, which is the financial education not taught in traditional schools.
Satori means a moment of enlightenment, which in finance is realizing that you can achieve an infinite return on investment and never need money again.
In 1973, Kiyosaki bought an $18,000 beachfront condo in Maui with a 10 percent credit card down payment, making a $25 infinite return.
In 1971, Nixon took the US off the gold standard, which the creator claims started the inflation of fake money and the decline of the middle class.
McDonalds makes its massive wealth through real estate holdings rather than just selling hamburgers.
content:
Robert Kiyosaki introduces Tom Wheelwright, a CPA and his personal tax advisor, who authored the book "Tax-Free Wealth." Kiyosaki notes that taxes are the single largest expense. He explains the background of "Rich Dad Poor Dad," a book that is fundamentally about accounting. Kiyosaki shares his background as a fourth-generation Japanese-American born in Hawaii. He explains that his poor dad was the head of education for the state of Hawaii and had a master's in accounting, but died broke. His rich dad was his best friend's father who never finished school because his own father died when he was 13, forcing him to take over the family business in real school with real teachers like accountants, bookkeepers, attorneys, bankers, and brokers.

Kiyosaki draws the Rich Dad Poor Dad diagram on a whiteboard, showing Income, Expense, Assets, and Liabilities, linked by Cash Flow. He explains that assets put money in your pocket and liabilities take money out of your pocket, such as buying houses that people think are assets but are actually liabilities. Next, he draws the Cash Flow Quadrant (CFQ), dividing business people into four categories: Employees (E), Self-Employed (S), Business Owners (B), and Investors (I). Tom Wheelwright explains the tax rates for each quadrant: Employees pay 40%, Self-Employed pay 60%, Business Owners with 500+ employees pay 20%, and Investors pay 0%. Kiyosaki notes that schools push people into the E and S quadrants, which have the highest tax brackets without financial education.

Tom Wheelwright explains that tax laws are a series of incentives created by the government to reward actions like creating employment, housing, hotels, agriculture, oil, and gas. The government offers huge tax breaks to the B and I quadrants because they do what the government needs done in the private market. Wheelwright mentions that the Trump tax cut reduced the corporate tax rate from 35% to 21% and provided large real estate deductions.

Kiyosaki discusses his career history, noting he was a marine helicopter pilot in Vietnam and attended an MBA program in Hawaii, where he asked his professor if he was an accountant and whether he had ever been an accountant. When the professor answered yes to the first and no to the second, Kiyosaki dropped out of the MBA program. He compares this to his time at the US Merchant Marine Academy at Kings Point, New York, where he studied oil and gas and became a tanker driver for Standard Oil of California.

Kiyosaki explains that money is created when you borrow, referencing Richard Nixon taking the US off the gold standard in 1971. He states that the rich get richer by using debt to buy assets, which reduces their taxes through depreciation and amortization. Wheelwright explains depreciation as a tax benefit reflecting wear and tear on buildings, which can provide large deductions even when buildings actually appreciate in value. Kiyosaki shares his first real estate seminar in 1973 on Maui, where he bought a $18,000 beachfront condo with a 10% credit card down payment, achieving an infinite return on investment (ROI). He defines ROI as Return on Information and Satori as a moment of enlightenment when you realize you can achieve an infinite return and never need money again.

Kiyosaki emphasizes that the rich do not save money; they save gold and silver and use debt to acquire assets. He mentions taking three resource companies public through the Toronto Stock Exchange (TSX): an oil company, an Argentine silver mine, and a Chinese gold company in Daliang, Province. He notes that his Chinese gold mine was later confiscated by the government, an example of country risk that is not taught in business school. Finally, Wheelwright promotes a free checklist of 12 questions a CPA should ask every client, available via a QR code and link in the description.
creator: Robert Kiyosaki and Tom Wheelwright
